issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette:
Harjit Singh is a 75-year-old potter who came to treatment at his wife’s urging after months of becoming smaller inside his own life. He and his family had come to the United States decades earlier as refugees after surviving political violence in Punjab. When he tries to tell it now, the worst part will not line up into a story. He can say there were uniforms, shouting, the sound of vehicles arriving too fast, and the sight of bodies being carried toward hurried burials, but the central terror comes back to him in flashes that are sharper than ordinary memory and yet impossible for him to explain from beginning to end. He remembers dirt, exhaust, a hand pulling him down, a policeman’s presence nearby, and the unbearable certainty that grief itself had become dangerous. The pieces do not fit together for him, and what unsettles him is how those fragments feel more immediate than the events of yesterday in his studio.

In the years since, certain moments have continued to seize him with that same sense of threat. If he passes a cemetery or hears of a funeral in the community, he feels his body tighten before he can think. The sound of cars outside, especially when one slows abruptly near the curb, can make him stop at the wheel and listen as if something is about to happen. A police cruiser on the street is enough to change the whole meaning of an afternoon. In those moments Harjit has come to believe he must be especially careful because danger can arrive without warning; he is certain that if he relaxes, he will be caught unprepared. He also reads his own reactions as proof that he is no longer the man he used to be. He had built a life through his hands, his steadiness, his patience at the wheel, but now even small upsets feel to him like evidence that he cannot cope.

That belief has changed the way he holds the past in mind. Because he sees himself as less capable and the world as requiring constant vigilance, he approaches the memories as something he cannot safely face or master. When he tries to describe what happened, his words falter and the memory breaks apart into sensory shards instead of narrative. He will fall silent, gesture vaguely, and say that it is all there but not sayable. The vividness of those fragments convinces him further that the danger is somehow still present rather than over, and because they come without order, funerals, cemeteries, car sounds, and police do not feel like reminders to him so much as openings through which the past rushes back in.

His work as a potter has become one of the places where this pattern is most visible. The studio sits near a road, and when he hears a car idle outside he looks up from the wheel and checks the door, the windows, the street beyond. If a patrol car passes, he cannot settle again for some time. He scans the room and the alley repeatedly, telling himself that anyone sensible would do the same. The same happens on days when a customer mentions a death in the family or asks for an urn; the image of graves and mourning catches him immediately, and by afternoon he feels confirmed in his private conviction that he cannot handle even minor disturbances anymore.

Over months, Harjit has organized his life around preventing that flood of memory. He avoids funerals, even for people he respected, and has stopped accompanying his wife to the cemetery on family anniversaries. He turns down invitations that might have brought pleasure—a grandchild’s celebration, a community gathering, an outing with old friends—because feeling light or hopeful now seems risky, as if letting down his guard would make him more vulnerable to being overwhelmed. He avoids disagreements in the studio and at home, backing away from even ordinary friction because he does not trust himself to tolerate the upset. These habits give him brief relief, but they have narrowed his world. His wife experiences him as distant and watchful; apprentices no longer stay long because he seems distracted, always listening past them for the street.

That shrinking of his life has only deepened his shame. Each funeral skipped, each happy occasion declined, each careful retreat from conflict becomes more evidence to him that he is no longer capable of the things that once defined him. And the smaller he makes his days, the more exposed he feels whenever he does encounter a trigger. A single siren or the sight of police near the market can undo the whole day. The memories come back in hard, bright fragments, and he responds by watching the environment even more closely and avoiding even more.

He finally agreed to seek help after refusing to attend the burial of an older cousin and then finding himself unable to return to the pottery wheel for two days because the scrape of cars outside the studio kept making him freeze. What frightened him most was not just the fear itself, but the sense that his life was being ruled by pieces of the past he could neither speak nor control. What he says he wants is simple: to be able to go with his wife where he chooses, to work with clay without constantly listening for danger, and to feel that a funeral, a passing car, or the sight of police belongs to the present instead of dragging him back into something that never seems fully over.
